If your workplace could have high radon levels, follow this process to manage the risk:

Assess the risk of high radon levels.

Measure radon levels in higher-risk premises.

Act on any high results.

Maintain any radon reduction measures, review changes to the premises or how they are used, and assess whether retesting is needed.

Assess

Employers must protect the health and safety of their employees and anyone else who may be affected by their work, so far as is reasonably practicable.

Under the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974 and Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999, employers must assess health and safety risks and take action to remove or control them. This includes carrying out a risk sufficient assessment and taking suitable actions.

As radon comes from the ground, underground areas are more likely to have high levels. UKHSA advises employers to identify radon as a workplace hazard if any of the following apply:

the workplace is in a radon Affected Area

there is a basement occupied for more than about 50 hours each year

workplace is wholly underground; such as mines, tunnels and caves

there may be internal sources of radon, such as geological samples or ground water

Employers should seek specialist advice from us for wholly underground workplaces and workplaces where there may be an internal source of radon.

The level radon in a building depends on its location, construction, amount of ventilation and how the building is used. Although work environments vary greatly, elevated radon levels can occur in almost any type of workplace.

Radon levels can vary significantly within the same building. An individual’s exposure depends on the radon levels in the areas where they spend most of their working time.

It is important to measure radon in locations that represent where employees spend most of their time within the building so that the assessment accurately reflects staff exposure. Read more about health risks of radon.

Measure

Testing is generally undertaken in ground floor rooms that are used routinely. Other rooms, on higher floors or those in which people spend little time, do not generally need to be tested. If your company occupies a shared building and not on the ground floor – you should test your lowest occupied level in the building which may be an upper storey.

If radon is an identified hazard, the workplace should be tested. Regulations apply if the radon level exceeds 300 Bq m⁻³ as an annual average in any area. The combination of the radon level, occupancy time and workplace type will determine what action is required.

Number of detectors to order

If you have many premises to test, consider how you are going to manage the logistics.

Workplace type Number of monitors Examples

Office, individual or small One per 100 m², generally corresponds to between a half and third of all ground floor rooms Banks, small shops, professional practice (solicitors, etc), residential homes, schools

Open plan office, and retail or workshop up to about 1000 m², also public access areas One per 250 m² Administrative and call centres, light industry, hotels

As above, up to 5000 m² One per 500 m² Large retail etc

Very large areas of several thousand m² One for each distinct area with obviously different environmental conditions, not less than 1 per 1000 m² Manufacturing or process plant, warehouses

Basements Should be monitored if occupied for more than 50 hours per year (~ an hour per week). One monitor for each occupied room, section or area. Basements with generally high occupancy should be monitored using the rules as for ground floors Retail, bank and professional storage areas

Wholly underground As a guide at least one in each main working area, and other normally occupied areas, but seek specialist advice Water industry, mines and caves

Effect of ventilation - In principle, radon may be prevented from accumulating in premises with particularly high influx of fresh air, but a measurement is still required unless a risk assessment can show that the radon level at a particular location is necessarily low at all times when it is occupied. Furthermore, there will often be adjoining or linked places, such as an office, store, computer area or access duct, with quite different conditions where a measurement would be required.

Downloadable version: Workplace radon detectors monitors - guidance table (PDF, 69.2 KB, 2 pages)

Act

If the annual average radon level in any part of a workplace exceeds 300 becquerels per cubic metre (Bq m⁻³), The Ionising Radiations Regulations 2017 (or The Ionising Radiations Regulations (Northern Ireland) 2017) apply.

In these circumstances, the employer must take action to protect staff and comply with legal requirements. Your UKHSA radon gas test report will include practical advice on the steps you could take to manage and reduce radon levels and meet regulatory requirements.

If radon levels are below the workplace threshold, employers should keep a record of the results and review them after around 10 years, or sooner if there are significant changes to the building’s structure or how the workplace is used.

Further guidance is available from the Health and Safety Executive (HSE).

Maintain

Radon levels can vary over time. This is usually because of changes to the construction of the building or alterations to heating and ventilation which can be caused by a change in use. For this reason:

radon should remain in your routine reviews of risk assessments

consider any changes and assess whether the test needs to be repeated

check radon levels annually, even if a radon reduction system is installed, as these systems can become less effective over time and may need maintenance or updates before they fail

Information to pass to employees
